stories.headline: Arsenal's Bruno Guimarães on unique penalty technique: 'Not working anymore'
stories.summary: Arsenal midfielder Bruno Guimarães has admitted that his penalty technique "is not working anymore," saying that he has to change the way he takes them in an exclusive interview with ESPN Brasil.
stories.body:
Arsenal midfielder Bruno Guimarães has admitted that his penalty technique "is not working anymore," saying that he has to change the way he takes them in an exclusive interview with ESPN Brasil.

Guimarães' stutter-step penalty style has come under the spotlight in recent weeks with the Brazilian's missed penalty the reason for Arsenal's shootout defeat to League Two Fleetwood Town in the Carabao Cup last week.

It joined an alarming recent record from the spot with Guimarães missing three out of his last four penalties for his club and country.

"Look, I think I've been taking my penalties in a certain way. I tried it during the World Cup, and I tried it here, too. It's clear to me now that it's not working anymore," Guimarães told ESPN Brasil.

"I'm humble enough to acknowledge that I need to improve and that I have to change the way I take them. But one thing is certain: this doesn't change who I am as a player or as a person.

"As I said, I'm humble enough to admit that my recent penalty kicks haven't been good. My record before the World Cup was very strong, but lately, I haven't been able to deliver at that same level. It's something I need to work on, I have to train differently.

"Life doesn't stop, and the challenges keep coming. We have another match this Sunday, and if I let this get to me, I'll only spiral downward.

"Or should I turn things around instead? I need to mature through my mistakes and learn from them. I've already decided that I shouldn't continue taking them the way I was."

Guimarães also said he takes "three or four" penalty kicks every training session as he aims to restore his positive spot-kick record.

"I think the most important thing is not to be afraid of what might happen, it's about putting in the work during training so that when the moment arrives, I'm ready," he said.

- Arsenal's Dowman handed three-game ban for red card after appeal rejected

"Every single day now, I take at least three or four penalty kicks, I want to be prepared in case it happens again. I can't let my teammates down, and I can't let our people down.

"We know it can happen [missing penalty kicks], we saw it at the World Cup, with Messi missing a penalty, Mbappé missing one, and plenty of others missing as well. It's obviously a situation we'd rather avoid, but I'm humble enough to recognize when something isn't going right.

"What I need to do is work even harder so that when the next opportunity comes along, I can step up and not let it go to waste."

stories.headline: How the Golden State Valkyries won the 2026 WNBA title in just two years
stories.summary: When Golden State joined the WNBA, the owner said the team would win a title within five years. The Valkyries did it in two.
stories.body:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Almost exactly two years ago, Natalie Nakase sat across from Golden State owner Joe Lacob for her job interview to become the head coach of the WNBA's newest team, the Valkyries. It was October 2024, and Nakase had walked into the interview with notes on why she would be the best fit, her vision for how to build a team and what set her apart from her colleagues.

But the first 10 minutes of the conversation were led by Lacob: He told Nakase he likes to set incredibly high goals and shared how he plans to achieve them. Nakase sat up straighter and leaned in a few inches closer, enticed by Lacob's work ethic.

Near the end of the conversation, Lacob told Nakase the ultimate goal, the same one he had shared in the news conference announcing the creation of the team a year earlier: "We're going to win a championship in five years."

She slammed her fists on the table in front of them.

"Hell yeah, we're gonna win a championship," she said.

On Saturday, the Golden State Valkyries did just that, beating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in Game 7 of the WNBA Finals to win their first title.

Lacob and Nakase were wrong about one thing, though. The Valkyries didn't win their first championship in five years. They did it in two.

"I walked out of that conversation with Joe like, 'I want to work for him,'" Nakase said. "More than that, I want to win that first championship for him."

After the interview, Nakase immediately called her mentors, asking them how she could deliver on Lacob's aspirations. Their biggest piece of advice was to build a clear culture, and do it with competitors who would sacrifice anything for the group.

Along with general manager Ohemaa Nyanin, Nakase set the identity she wanted for her team: scrappy, defensive-minded, no egos. The Valkyries built the team their way, facing external scrutiny nearly every step of the way. People gawked -- or even laughed -- at Lacob's proclamation. But Nakase stood strong in her belief, and in his.

Sitting next to the championship trophy with a beer in her hand Saturday, Nakase was asked if winning the title felt as she imagined it would.

"F--- yeah."

TOGETHER, NYANIN AND Nakase handpicked the players who make up Golden State's roster. During the 2024 expansion draft, the Valkyries acquired Veronica Burton, the gritty two-way guard, and Kayla Thornton, a reigning WNBA champion -- two cornerstones of the franchise -- as well as Cecilia Zandalasini, an Italian national. Tiffany Hayes, a former Sixth Player of the Year, signed in free agency, and Janelle Salaun, a French forward, signed on a training camp roster. The Valkyries used their No. 5 pick in 2025 on Juste Jocyte -- a 19-year-old from Lithuania who stayed overseas that year.

Again, their decisions were questioned. Without a star, and without a history of any success, external expectations for the Valkyries were low.

But in the 2025 postseason, this group made history, propelling the Valkyries to become the first expansion franchise in WNBA history to make the playoffs in its first season. The Valkyries were swept by the Minnesota Lynx in the first round, but it laid the foundation for what the team could build on, and made Golden State an attractive landing place for free agents.

For more than a year, the Valkyries knew whom they wanted to prioritize. Gabby Williams was part of Nyanin's original vision of the team, and Nakase met with Williams in 2025 in Turkey to pitch her on coming to Golden State. But the Seattle Storm cored Williams that offseason, guaranteeing Seattle exclusive negotiating rights with the French national. Williams remembers when she heard Lacob make his proclamation in 2023. "I was impressed, and I was enticed. It was like, this is a team I could want to play for one day," Williams said. "I thought I would finish my career in Seattle, but hearing that made me think a little bit. This guy is not playing around; he wants to win. That was eye-opening to me."

When Williams became a free agent, the Valkyries contacted her again, and Lacob joined Nakase and Nyanin in the recruitment.

"He said, 'This is why we are going to win. This is why it would be silly for you to go anywhere else. This is why we're going to have longevity. I want to build dynasties here,'" Williams said.

"Who doesn't want to come to something like that? We play this game to win championships. I've never won one, and at this point in my career, that is the top priority. ... I was so convinced that I would not win anywhere else."

One day after signing Williams, the Valkyries made another trajectory-shifting acquisition, landing Kiah Stokes after she spent four seasons and won three titles with Las Vegas, where she played alongside A'ja Wilson every day and under Nakase for one year. After Iliana Rupert announced that she would miss the 2026 season due to pregnancy, Stokes started every game, defending Angel Reese in the Finals.

Nyanin knew that these players could unlock a new level of her team. What has surprised the GM, though, is how quickly it has come together.

"You just never know if that's going to work out," Nyanin said.

It has. Williams, who was named Finals MVP thanks to a 30-point performance in Game 7, is having the best season of her career. She averaged a career-best 14.4 points and shot 34.2% from 3 -- and also finished second in Defensive Player of the Year voting and received WNBA All-Defensive first-team honors. She became the engine for Golden State's top-ranked defense, while also stepping up to be the shotmaker the Valkyries needed.

"The best part has been coming to work every day and enjoying it. Like, actually, that's a huge part of contending," Williams said. "When the playoffs started, our motivation was just -- we didn't want to stop playing together. We wanted to go as deep as we could because we knew this is the last time we could have a group like this. It's been really healing for me. It's made this season really special."

Down late in a win-or-go-home Game 3 in the first round against the Dallas Wings, Thornton pulled Burton, Williams and Kaila Charles into a huddle beneath their basket. They put their arms around each other and took a collective breath.

"It's just one of those things where [it was] an awareness of what we need," Burton said. "And in that moment, we needed to take an exhale and be together and just be present. ... That's pouring into each other and building each other up."

As Nyanin watched from the tunnel -- and as that sigh fueled their comeback and offered a glimpse of the composure Golden State, a team with no All-WNBA player selections, has possessed since its inception, Nyanin knew that all of the pieces she put together fit perfectly.

"That was the epitome of things we have said to them here and there," Nyanin said. "In that moment, all of the little things we have put together, I took a breath as well just to say yes, they will fight with each other and for each other. That's exactly why I am doing the job I am doing."

NAKASE WOULDN'T LET her players pick up a ball for the first three days of training camp this season.

There was no shooting, no running plays, no offense. The first three days of camp were dedicated to defense.

"That's when I knew this was going to be different," Burton said.

Those early sessions set the tone for what Nakase would demand: consistent defensive intensity, attention to detail and execution on the game plan. It also gave her players a taste of the kind of coach she is -- one who plays battle sounds during practice and calls her players "killers," doesn't allow for celebrations, and believes that cursing just means you're telling the truth.

Even when Nakase's behavior seems jarring -- or as she puts it, extreme -- she has built an environment that encourages her players to speak up and feel respected. It's why they so willingly buy into Nakase's vision and style.

"She's so authentic," Williams said. "We know her intentions are to put us in the best position to win. ... She's passionate. And sometimes we laugh at her, but we also check on her ... it's the love we have for each other."

When Williams arrived in Golden State, she told Nakase that sometimes her delivery was confusing. Others have told Nakase that they needed more time to celebrate the smaller wins. Her coaching staff urged her to take more care of herself so she can be a better leader.

All of this experience has led the Valkyries here, to their first title. Nakase's focus on defense made Golden State's unit the top ranked in the league through the regular season -- holding opponents to a league-low 75.1 points per game -- and second best in the playoffs. Stokes had 31 blocked shots this postseason, tied with Lisa Leslie for the most in WNBA history.

And her players' feedback has pushed Nakase to be a better version of herself -- and helped turn around the Finals when Golden State trailed 2-1. After the first three games of the series, she gave herself an F-minus score on her coaching because her communication was poor. So she turned to her players to see how she -- and in turn they -- could be better.

"You can give the best scheme in the world, but if your players don't want to follow it, it's not going to be successful," Stokes said. "Her willingness to listen to us and our ideas about what we think we're best at and what we can do, that's one thing that has jumped out to me; her willingness to adapt to her players."

Heading into Game 4, Nakase inserted Hayes and Kaila Charles into the starting lineup in place of Thornton and Zandalasini, respectively. Charles finished the game with a plus-14, and Hayes added 13 points -- and the change led to a massive momentum shift in the series, with the Valkyries taking the next two games.

"The best thing about our team is no one cares who starts, no one cares," Nakase said. "We can do that because we have a really selfless team, ego-less team."

"She's a great coach for a reason," Charles. "We trust our coach, so whatever she sees, we'll execute."

As Nakase walked out of her first interview with Lacob, she pledged to herself not to let his WNBA team fail. When she began to work alongside Nyanin, she promised her that they wouldn't let each other fail. As she opened up each season with her players, Nakase made sure they had every piece of support they needed.

All of this has led to history, and the Valkyries winning a title far sooner than anyone -- even Lacob -- could have ever predicted.

"Of course this is unbelievable," Lacob said Saturday night as the Valkyries celebrated. "Two years? It's insane."

stories.headline: Artturi Lehkonen and Cale Makar lead the Avalanche to a 5-2 victory over the Flames
stories.summary: — Artturi Lehkonen scored twice, Nathan MacKinnon had a goal and an assist, and the Colorado Avalanche beat the Calgary Flames 5-2 on Saturday night.
stories.body:
DENVER -- — Artturi Lehkonen scored twice, Nathan MacKinnon had a goal and an assist, and the Colorado Avalanche beat the Calgary Flames 5-2 on Saturday night.


Martin Necas and Brock Nelson also scored, and defenseman Cale Makar had four assists for the Avalanche. Mackenzie Blackwood made 25 saves.


Colorado has won two in a row against opponents playing on the second night of a back-to-back. The Avalanche defeated New Jersey on Wednesday and faced Calgary’s No. 3 goaltender, Arsenii Sergeev, less than 24 hours after the Flames beat Seattle.


Joel Farabee and Martin Pospisil scored for Calgary. Sergeev made 29 saves in his second career start and first this season.


Sergeev was recalled from the AHL when the Flames placed Devin Cooley on the injured list with a lower-body injury.


Colorado was not whistled for a penalty, while Calgary took three — two on a double minor late in the third period.


The Avalanche, who lost defenseman Josh Manson for two months after he injured an ankle against the Devils, saw Nelson exit in the second when he took a shot by Makar off the side of his helmet.


Nelson, who scored earlier in the period, was able to skate to the bench and down the tunnel. He returned in the third period.


Nelson capped a three-goal burst in the first 10 minutes of the second that gave Colorado a 4-0 lead. Farabee scored 1:43 after Nelson’s goal, and Pospisil made it 4-2 when he scored 1:59 into the third.


Lehkonen deflected Makar’s shot from the point at 4:09 to make it 5-2.


Two of Blackwood's stops came after MacKinnon made it 1-0 late in the first. Blackwood made a sprawling glove save on Matt Coronato with 8.5 seconds left in the period and then stopped Farabee 12 seconds into the second.


Up next
Flames: At the San Jose Sharks on Monday night.


Avalanche: At the Chicago Blackhawks on Monday night.

stories.headline: Fernando Alonso's blunt response to Mexico City Grand Prix qualifying: 'Frustration beyond imagination'
stories.summary: Fernando Alonso gave a terse eight-word interview after suffering "frustration beyond imagination" when engine trouble appeared to cost Aston Martin a major opportunity in qualifying at the Mexico City Grand Prix.
stories.body:
Fernando Alonso gave a terse eight-word interview after suffering "frustration beyond imagination" when engine trouble appeared to cost Aston Martin a major opportunity in qualifying at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Alonso had been 0.7 seconds off the lead in FP2 -- a rare margin for Aston Martin this season -- and had posted an early competitive lap in Q1, before being told to park up his car in the stadium section of the track.

The two-time world champion protested the decision and onboards showed him gesticulating angrily inside the cockpit as he stopped and as he got out of the car.

He was not in a talkative mood by the time he got to the media pen in the paddock.

The transcript of his interview with F1 TV went as follows:

Question: "Any idea what happened yet?"

Alonso: "Engine."

Question: "It looked like it was a big opportunity this weekend?"

Alonso: "It was."

Question: "The car's been looking good all weekend..."

Alonso: "Correct."

Question: "I can sense the frustration. Anything you can do from the back?"

Alonso: "Not from the back."

Alonso then walked away from the interview.

The Spaniard will start from 18th on the grid.

Aston Martin later confirmed that the team detected a suspected water pressure issue linked to the ERS system (Energy Recovery System), meaning they had to stop the car.

- Mexico City Grand Prix: Lewis Hamilton takes first Ferrari pole, Kimi Antonelli in fifth

- Kimi Antonelli's solution to feeling 'tense' while on brink of title: 'Bombard myself with melatonin'

- Lewis Hamilton 'special' first Ferrari pole at Mexico City GP a reminder of Michael Schumacher's success

The team came into F1's new regulations dreaming of breaking out of the grid's midfield and making the big five, but it arrived in 2026 miles off the pace with new engine partner Honda.

Alonso spoke in more detail to the written press shortly afterwards.

He explained that he had wanted to come back to the pits to fix the issue and potentially stay in the session.

"I was 100 metres away from the garage, but probably the problem was bigger than anything possible to do in the garage," he said. "So, yeah, the safest thing for everyone else also on track was to stop and I followed the instructions."

He added: "There is not much we can do, and I think we lost a big opportunity. So, yeah, frustration is beyond imagination, but this is the story of the year."

The Aston Martin has struggled to match the power output of rival manufacturers this year -- Alonso suggested the layout of the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez was perfect to score a morale-boosting result.

Asked why the car had looked stronger here, he said: "Less straights. There are two straights only into [Turn] 1, into [Turn] 4. The rest, with the level of grip so low, you hardly can go full throttle. So it is less power sensitive here."

stories.headline: Chris Fagan to join the Blues as director of coaching in 2027
stories.summary: Triple premeirship coach Chris Fagan has made the call on his AFL future, joining Carlton as their director of coaching for 2027.
stories.body:
Triple premeirship coach Chris Fagan has made the call on his AFL future, joining Carlton as their director of coaching for 2027.

The 65-year-old stepped down as Brisbane's senior coach after the club's 2026 premiership win -- it's third in a row -- with an aim to return closer to family.

Announced by the Blues on Saturday morning, Fagan will oversee a matchday role and begin mentoring the coaching panel to "establish development pathways for the coaches and help drive an elite, sustainable football program".

Fagan said he was looking forward to making a "real impact" at the Blues.

"While I loved my 10 years as a Senior Coach, this is a role I am passionate about and where I know I can have a real impact in this next phase of my football career," Fagan said in a statement.

"Supporting people to get the absolute best out of themselves is what I love most about football, so the chance to now be able to do that on a full-time basis is incredibly exciting. I can't wait to connect with each person in the football department, and in particular work closely with Josh to help every coach and player be the best Carlton person they can possibly be.

"In all my conversations with [the club] before accepting the role, what resonated strongly was how aligned they were on how to make Carlton a great football club. They shared a clear vision of evolving Carlton into a club that can contend but most importantly, they understand there is still significant work to do to get there.

"To have the senior leadership of a football club share such clarity in their direction, combined with a role that gives me genuine purpose, makes joining Carlton an opportunity too good to pass up."

Meanwhile Carlton's GM of Football Chris Davies said the appointment was an important one to support first-time senior coach Josh Fraser.

"We want to build our football club around good people and they do not come any better than Chris Fagan," Davies said.

"Few in the game have his wealth of experience and ability to connect with and get the best out of those around him. Most importantly, he is a proven winner who knows what it takes to build a consistently high-performing environment.

"Chris and Josh have built a connection in recent weeks over a shared philosophy of putting people first and building a program the right way. With Chris on board, Josh will be well supported, our coaches will be well developed and our program will continue to build the clarity and discipline required to be truly elite.

"We can't wait to welcome Chris and his wife Ursula, their daughters Jessica and Ellen and the entire Fagan family to Carlton."

...more to come.

stories.headline: Man City, Bayern among the good, bad and lucky in Europe's top leagues
stories.summary: We're a quarter of the way through the 2026-27 European season -- long enough to separate fact from fiction when it comes to from. Who's been lucky? Who's been good? Who's been both, or neither?
stories.body:
About a quarter of the way through the club season, your place in the table only means so much. In the Premier League and Bundesliga, 14 teams -- including Ipswich Town, Paderborn and even Tottenham Hotspur -- are within six points of the top four. In Ligue 1, it's 13. In LaLiga, 14 teams are within six points of the relegation zone. You can find some separation here and there, but we're just getting started, and we only have a partial picture of how things will end up.

We also know that the table is lying a little bit. We see funky results all the time, and they have an outsized impact when we're seen only a small portion of matches. Still, by this point in the 2026-27 campaign, each Big Five team has played hundreds and hundreds of possessions, and we know who is creating (or allowing) the best chances. Thanks to xG, we also know what that means.

Essentially, xG is a chance creation metric. It obviously doesn't guarantee success, especially in the short term, but over the long haul a team's ability to create superior shot quality and/or volume is more predictive than simply who's putting the ball in the net in a small sample. And by comparing who's generated the most points to who's created chance creation advantages, with a fun trend line in between, we can get a grasp of who is ahead of or behind where they should be.

Who's both lucky and good? Who's good, but unlucky? Who's the opposite?

Here are some xG standouts, for better or worse, in Europe's Big Five leagues.

- Jones: Vozinha's Ballon d'Or appearance was made for us

- Ogden: Man United are a mess. Where are the Glazers?

- Olley: Ballon d'Or is Kane's crowning moment

Lucky and good

Definition: Teams with an xG differential of at least +0.3 per game, but more points than expected

Lazio. Lazio have finished seventh or worse in Serie A for three straight years, and due to an ongoing fan protest of club president Claudio Lotito, they're averaging a league-worst home attendance of 9,515. They've also only dropped two points in nine league matches, and they're tied with Inter atop the table. Pretty wild stuff.

It's also probably unsustainable stuff.

While they've enjoyed a few genuinely dominant performances (like a 6-2 win at Sassuolo), they've also scored 22 goals from shots worth just 15.5 xG. Forward Tijjani Noslin, winger Gustav Isaksen and midfielder Kenneth Taylor have combined for nine goals from 3.9 xG; I probably don't have to spell out how unsustainable that is. Lazio have stockpiled enough points to remain in the Champions League hunt for a while, but there's a goal-scoring slump in their future, whether or not there are fans in the stands to see it.

Atletico Madrid. Diego Simeone scoffs at your advanced stats. Over the past 12 full seasons, Atletico have produced a goal differential higher -- and in some cases, much higher -- than their xG differential 11 times. In fact, over the Simeone era, their GD in league play (+504) is 46% higher than their xGD (+346.0). Dark magic is a real thing, I guess.

Atleti have always been happy allowing opponents to hammer shots into a box cluttered by defenders (with the immaculate Jan Oblak behind them), and they've always had impressive finishers -- Antoine Griezmann (143 goals from 113.6 xG) and Angel Correa (68 from 57.4) in particular -- ready to turn a half-chance into a goal. But even without either Griezmann or Correa, they're overachieving again this fall. Oblak remains excellent, Álex Baena has picked up the "major finishing overachiever" mantle, and in four matches with a negative xG differential, Atleti have scored two wins, a draw and only one loss.

Manchester City. No one else has been Lazio-level lucky this season, but City damn near packed a season's worth of xG fortune into one match -- a 5-3 win over Sunderland in which they generated 2.8 xG and allowed 3.6. It was their only match with a negative xG differential this season, but between that and a 1-0 win over Manchester United (xGD: +0.1), they could have easily dropped more points than they actually have this season.

They have an xG cheat code in habitually excellent finisher Erling Haaland (nine goals from shots worth 6.1), but they've been lucky that their defense (seventh in xG allowed) hasn't been more costly.

Borussia Dortmund. It's been difficult to get a read on BVB this season. They've generated a positive xG differential in all seven Bundesliga matches, and their only losses have come against Bayern in the Franz Beckenbauer Super Cup and at Bodø/Glimt in their North Pole fortress in the Champions League. But after winning six straight before the international break, they sandwiched a pair of frustrating draws around the Bodø/Glimt loss upon their return.

Dortmund are on the lucky-and-good list because their defense has been a bit too successful. They've allowed goals in just two Bundesliga matches, and their four goals allowed have come from shots worth 7.3 xG. Yes, they have a high-level goalkeeper in Gregor Kobel, but opponents have simply missed the target quite a bit, too. That likely won't continue, nor will their current tie with Bayern in the league table.

Como. Como are easily Serie A's happiest Champions League story thus far, having won two of their first three matches in their debut in the competition. In theory, they've balanced those duties with solid league play, too -- they're fourth in the league and only five points from first. But they've been at least a little bit fortunate: They've suffered a negative xG differential in four of nine Serie A matches, but they've won two of those four and drawn in one.

- Who are Como? The vacation-destination club that just rocked Man United

That said, the trends are strong: Since returning from the international break, they've suffered a negative xGD only once and have taken 10 points from four league matches. Including their Champions League stomping of Manchester United, they've generated an xGD of at least plus-1.1 in three straight. They were lucky and good, but they might just be good now.

Good, but unlucky

Definition: Teams with an xG differential of at least +0.3 per game and fewer points than expected

Nottingham Forest. If you didn't look at the table, you'd think Oliver Glasner is doing great work in his first season as manager in Nottingham. Forest beat Aston Villa and drew with Liverpool at Anfield, and for the season they're sixth in xG created (13.4), second in xG allowed (9.0) and fifth in overall xG differential. The fundamentals are in great shape.

Somehow they're also 18th in the table, behind even Glasner's direction-less former employer, Crystal Palace. They've turned shots worth 13.4 xG into only six goals; attackers Morgan Gibbs-White, Liam Delap and Chris Wood have attempted 38 shots worth 5.3 xG, but they've put only eight shots on target and scored twice. Forest have generated a positive xG differential in six of eight matches and have somehow won just one of them. That they will almost certainly right the ship in this regard and start winning matches soon, but how many unnecessary points will they have dropped by then?

Brest. After surging to third in Ligue 1 in 2023-24 and qualifying for the Champions League, Brest slipped to ninth and then 12th in the last two seasons. Now they're 13th. It appears the balloon is losing helium.

If the results start matching the chance creation, however, a turnaround is possible. They're second in Ligue 1 in xG differential, well behind PSG but well ahead of everyone else. They've created a dominant xG differential of +1.9 or better in four matches but have somehow won only one of them. Both their finishing and defense have let them down at times, but midfielder Joris Chotard is fifth in the league in chances created, and the combo of young wingers Kamory Doumbia and Pathé Mboup with veteran big man Ludovic Ajorque has created a number of dangerous opportunities.

This is one of France's better teams, no matter what the table says.

Villarreal. Villarreal are third in xG differential and 10th in LaLiga. They have dropped unlikely points to Atletico Madrid (2-2 draw, +2.8 xG differential), Elche (0-0 draw, +2.1 xGD) and Alaves (1-0 loss, +1.0). Forwards Georges Mikautadze and Ayoze Pérez have scored just four goals from shots worth 8.4 xG; in the Champions League, meanwhile, they've scored two goals from 1.2.

Aside from finishing, there's nothing inherently wrong with this squad. They're third in shots per possession margin and fourth in xG per shot margin. They play a pretty possession game -- Renato Veiga is one of only two players in LaLiga (along with Barcelona's Gerard Martín) to already have over 100 progressive passes and 100 progressive carries -- without giving up much on the counter. But they're eight points behind fourth-place Real Betis; they have some ground to make up.

Bournemouth. Only Manchester City, Arsenal and Brentford have led more Premier League matches this season than Bournemouth, but somehow the Cherries have turned leads in six matches -- and positive xG differentials in six matches -- into just two wins. Marcus Tavernier has scored a lovely five goals from shots worth 3.6 xG, but the rest of the team has just six goals from shots worth 10.9. They aren't generating the sizable advantages they should, and they've been outscored 4-0 from the 80th minute on. They're third in xG differential but 13th in the table because of the late leaks.

It could be worse -- most of their unfortunate results have been draws and not losses. But with so many bigger clubs struggling out of the gate, Bournemouth had a chance to establish a good spot in the race for a top-five finish. They're off of that pace.

Bayern Munich. Maybe one day this hard-luck club will catch a break. Alas, the 35-time German champions have dropped points twice -- 0-0 at Schalke (xG differential: +1.7), 2-2 at Augsburg (+2.5) -- despite dominating the early stages of the season as much as ever.

Seriously, though, this is ridiculous:

Every so often, the Bundesliga figures out how to balance great crowds, fun stories and sustained challenges for Bayern, but it doesn't appear this will be one of those years, even if those two draws mean Bayern and Borussia Dortmund are tied in points at the moment. Bayern's xGD is actually higher now than it was after they won their first seven matches last season.

Ballon d'Or winner (!) Harry Kane has gone through his version of a finishing funk (he has four league goals from shots worth 5.2 xG), and Serge Gnabry is in a similar boat (one goal from 2.2 xG). Something tells me they'll be all right.

Bad, but unlucky

Definition: Teams with an xG differential worse than minus-0.3 per game and fewer points than expected

Venezia. It's a yo-yo period in Venice. Venezia were promoted from Serie B in 2021, but went straight back down. They came back up in 2024, went back down in 2025, then came right back up in 2026. And through eight matchdays, they have three points and are last in the Serie A table.

However, they haven't been that bad. This team obviously isn't loaded with proven finishers, but scoring just six goals from shots worth 14.5 xG is severely unfortunate. Forwards John Yeboah, Albion Rrahmani and Lion Lauberbach somehow have one goal from 5.1 xG; they aren't generating ridiculously high-quality shots, but that is still some unsustainably poor finishing. Venezia have generated a positive xG differential in four of nine matches, and they're 14th overall in xGD. They'll have a chance to stay up if their finishing begins to reflect their actual chance creation.

Borussia Mönchengladbach. The five-time German champions finally notched a win last weekend, shocking Stuttgart 3-2. It was both deserving and a long time coming. They had lost their first six league matches, alternating between awful (losing to RB Leipzig and Freiburg by a combined 8-0) and unlucky (4-3 losses to Elversberg and Mainz despite a combined xGD of +0.5).

The club hired former St. Pauli manager Alexander Blessin on Sept. 22, and while he made an immediate impact on their defense, they finally generated some offense in Stuttgart too. American right midfielder Joe Scally and 17-year old left midfielder Wael Mohya each had a goal and an assist in that match, and if Gladbach can generate production like that from the wings, maybe it will offset the black hole of production they've gotten from their center forwards in the absence of injured veteran Tim Kleindienst.

Valencia. After pulling nine points from their first 11 league matches last year and 10 from their first 15 in 2024-25, Valencia have just six points after 10 matches this season. Only Villarreal and Osasuna have been worse at finishing the season: Valencia have turned shots worth 10.8 xG into only seven goals. In matches against Real Betis (1-0 loss), Celta Vigo (0-0 draw) and Athletic Club (0-0 draw) they attempted 40 shots worth 3.3 xG, and none went in the net. Those matches could have easily produced six to nine points ... but yielded just two instead.

Despite average defensive numbers, there's no way to say this team is anything better than below average. But while they're growing awfully familiar to relegation scraps at the moment -- and if you play with fire enough, you will get burned -- I can't say they're actually relegation-worthy just yet.

Troyes. Back in Ligue 1 after a three-year absence, Troyes attempt more shots than their opponents and press frequently. They don't attempt many good shots, but they rank 15th in xG created and 10th in xG allowed. That they only have five points from eight matches is therefore a smidgen unlucky. They've scored only five goals from shots worth 9.7 xG, and they've allowed 16 goals from shots worth 13.2. A lot of that damage comes from one match -- a 6-2 loss to Strasbourg in which both teams generated 2.9 xG -- but forwards Renaud Ripart and Jeremy Le Douaron have combined for two goals on 4.7 xG. Finish at more normal levels, and they'll have a solid shot at survival.

Sunderland. Sunderland were the "stats don't matter" team of 2025-26, ranking 18th in the Premier League in xG differential, but somehow finishing seventh and grabbing a spot in the Europa League. You usually don't have to wait long for what we'll call statistical comeuppance. This year they've actually improved to 15th in xG differential, and they've generated a positive xGD in four of eight matches, but they've won just one because aside from Brian Brobbey (three goals from shots worth 3.2 xG), no one can turn shots into goals.

Sunderland rank third in the league in xG per shot, but they're 18th in goals and haven't scored in a league match since Sept. 20. That puts them at the bottom of the table. A lot of teams are struggling at the moment, so they're not in too big a hole, but after this weekend's trip to Coventry City, their schedule gets awfully tricky.

Lucky and bad

Definition: Teams with an xG differential worse than minus-0.3 per game but more points than expected

Frosinone. Frosinone have been promoted to Serie A four times since 2015; they have yet to avoid going straight back down. That they're currently sixth in points per game, ahead of mighty Juventus, is a thrilling story. But it's really hard to believe this story will last. They're also 18th in xG differential, having scored 17 goals from shots worth 13.1 xG while allowing 13 goals from shots worth 19.5.

This is unsustainable in obvious ways, but as Sunderland learned last year, if you stockpile points early, you can ride it out when regression to the mean invariably hits. They're already nine points above the drop zone with a game in hand; from here, it won't take too much additional good fortune for them to survive a year in Serie A for the first time.

Elversberg. The most delightful early Bundesliga story is also a fortunate one. Tiny Elversberg, from a town of 13,000 people, have three wins and 10 points from seven matches in their top-division debut. They're a healthy eighth in the table, but they also have yet to actually generate a positive xG differential in a match, and in three one-goal wins they scored 11 goals from shots worth 7.4 xG.

This is an optimistic team with fun attacking ideas, and maybe they can continue to avoid the relegation hunt with bursts of excellence from players such as 22-year-old David Mokwa (1.2 xG, two goals) and 21-year-old Maurice Krattenmacher (2.4 xG, three goals). But they lost 4-0 to RB Leipzig last weekend, and it feels like there might be a few more heavy defeats in their future. Hopefully I'm wrong.

Marseille. Not only are Marseille a terribly disappointing eighth in Ligue 1 at the moment, but they're lucky to even be that high. Their 18 goals scored (first in the league) have come from just 13.6 xG (seventh), while their 18.5 xG allowed (last) has turned into only 13 goals (11th). Last week's 4-3 win over Le Havre featured a minus-1.6 xG differential.

Only Strasbourg have a lower league xG differential than l'OM right now. Marseille do have historically solid finishers like Amine Gouiri and Igor Paixão pacing the attack, and a lot of their defensive overachievement came from a single match -- a 2-1 loss to PSG in which they allowed shots worth 5.1 xG. Still, the fundamentals do not suggest that manager Bruno Genesio is fielding a team worth a spot in a European competition at the moment.

Cagliari. Like Frosinone, Cagliari has stocked up on some early points (13 in nine Serie A matches) thanks to some early good fortune. They've suffered a negative xG differential in six of nine matches, but have won two of those with a draw. They've gotten spectacular goalkeeping from Elia Caprile thus far, but allowing just 13 goals from shots worth 17.3 xG is pretty fortunate.

Strangely, though, it's offset some poor finishing from Cagliari, too: While left winger Daniel Maldini is on a hot streak (five goals from shots worth 3.4 xG), the rest of the team has just three goals from 8.1 xG, and if their own finishing progresses more than opponents', they could remain mid-table for quite a while longer.

Newcastle United. Let's isolate that PPG vs. xGD chart above with just Premier League teams.

Maybe no attack in Europe has defied xG more than Newcastle's, and in two different directions.

- Yoane Wissa: 1 goal from shots worth 3.0 xG (minus-2.0 difference)

- Everyone else: 11 goals from shots worth 6.2 xG (plus-4.8 difference)

Wissa has done a great job of generating nearly one-third of Newcastle's xG by himself, but he's been in a major finishing slump. And it's been more than offset by the fact that other guys can't seem to miss.

Newcastle ranks 16th in shots per possession margin and 19th in xG per shot margin; they've generated a positive xG differential in only one match, but incredibly, they lost that match and have only lost two of seven with a negative xGD. It either works (two of three wins were by two goals) or really, really doesn't (two of three losses were by three goals). And I honestly don't have much of an idea of what to expect from them moving forward. I'm not incredibly optimistic, though.

stories.headline: WNBA playoffs history: Notable records, stats, facts
stories.summary: During the WNBA playoffs, players are primed for greatness as they pursue championships. Check out our roundup of playoff records and stats now.
stories.body:
As the summer winds down, WNBA action picks up. The league's top teams begin the playoff journey to decide which group of 12 women will be crowned the queens of the court.

The WNBA playoffs have set the stage for some of the most memorable moments and performances in women's basketball history since the Houston Comets won the league's inaugural championship in 1997. Led by four-time WNBA Finals MVP Cynthia Cooper, the now-defunct Comets won the league's first four titles. They remain the only team to win at least three straight.

stories.headline: Spooky scheduling: How MLS ensures fans, players don't have horror Halloween
stories.summary: Everyone has Halloween plans, so to make sure players and fans could celebrate, MLS gave clubs the option of playing outside of trick-or-treat primetime.
stories.body:
Whether you're mapping out your neighborhood's notorious king-size candy hot spots for an epic evening of trick-or-treating, painstakingly sewing and gluing every last minute detail of your Jedi garb to win the night's costume competition, or simply need any excuse to dress up for a late night on the town, Halloween is the one night of the year when you can count on folks having plans. And that includes MLS players.

Almost without fail, every Saturday of the league seasons, games kick off at 7:30 p.m. local. But, MLS confirmed to ESPN, when the 2026 regular-season schedule was being created, it went to its clubs with a question: On Halloween, would you rather play earlier in the day, or even on Sunday, to free up your evening for other plans?

As a result, there's just one game beginning at MLS' standard start time: the Colorado Rapids will host the Chicago Fire in Denver's prime-time trick-or-treating window. And while supporters may forgo pillowcases full of candy to attend, the Rapids are sending fans home with a five-pound bag of potatoes as part of Fan Appreciation Night at Dick's Sporting Goods Park.

The other eight games taking place Saturday will begin at 1 p.m. or 2 p.m. local, with another six games slated for Sunday.

New York City FC is one of the seven clubs to host a 2 p.m. kickoff, which means Keaton Parks will have plenty of time to get into costume. The 29-year-old Texas native is affectionately known as "Big Bird," which is what he dressed up as for last year's festivities. Now he'll have a few extra hours to make sure his feathers look fabulous this Halloween.

Nashville SC cleared its whole day, electing to welcome Red Bull New York for a Sunday matinee. That frees up the afternoon of United States goalkeeper Brian Schwake, who's planning on an early evening of trick-or-treating with his young son.

stories.headline: Kimi Antonelli's solution to feeling 'tense' while on brink of title: 'Bombard myself with melatonin'
stories.summary: A tense, unwell and tired Kimi Antonelli has said he will "bombard myself with melatonin" to ensure himself a full night's sleep before the Mexico City Grand Prix, where he can become Formula 1's youngest world champion on Sunday.
stories.body:
A tense, unwell and tired Kimi Antonelli said he will "bombard myself with melatonin" to ensure himself a full night's sleep before the Mexico City Grand Prix, where he can become Formula 1's youngest world champion.

Antonelli qualified fifth, which became fourth after Max Verstappen's grid penalty, for a race where he will guarantee himself the title with a ninth-place finish or better.

Title rivals Lewis Hamilton and George Russell locked out the front row of the grid but Antonelli's fate is still in his own hands.

Should Hamilton win Sunday's race, the fight would go on another week to Brazil if Antonelli was 10th or lower.

The 20-year-old comes into the biggest race of his life not at 100%.

He missed Thursday's media duties on Thursday due to illness.

"I feel very tired to be fair, I still haven't recovered completely," said Antonelli, who admitted he's also been distracted by the chatter about what he can achieve at this race.

"It hasn't been an easy weekend, you know, and definitely I've been a bit more tense than usual, especially, you know, when you keep hearing wherever you go, any time of the day, the same thing, and people telling that it's already done. Knowing myself, I've been trying to block as much as possible this noise, but it hasn't been easy and definitely I've been a bit more tense today."

His plan to arrive at the race championship-ready is to do whatever it takes to have a full night's sleep.

He added: "I'm going to bombard myself with melatonin, so hopefully I will sleep a good 10 hours, hopefully. Just going to try to relax as much as possible, my family has just arrived, so it's going to be good to have them here. Just going to try to disconnect as much as possible, good sleep, and then ready for tomorrow."

- Mexico City Grand Prix: Lewis Hamilton takes first Ferrari pole, Kimi Antonelli in fifth

- 'Close to perfection,' 'A very big heart' - what F1 rivals think of boy-king Kimi Antonelli

- Lewis Hamilton 'special' first Ferrari pole at Mexico City GP a reminder of Michael Schumacher's success

Antonelli's thumping United States Grand Prix win last weekend moved him to within an inch of the title, but he arrived in Mexico under the weather.

Asked how he felt on Thursday, Antonelli said: "Very bad. I had a high fever and stomach problems, so it hasn't been easy. But now I feel OK, just low on energy, just feel pretty tired, so it's going to be important to try and sleep well, because I haven't been sleeping well in these days, and hopefully tomorrow I will have more energy."

The midweek illness meant Antonelli felt off the normal standard he's set in 2026 when qualifying started.

"I'm aware that definitely I haven't been driving well," he said. "I felt like already going to qualifying, I didn't feel great, and I felt a bit low on energy, so definitely, you know, it's not an excuse, but for sure, it hasn't been my finest performance."

Asked if he was feeling tense in Austin in the same way, he said: "No, Austin I wasn't driving tense, Austin I was much more relaxed. Definitely it's been a thing of this weekend."

stories.headline: Dodgers executive Bob Wolfe shifting to advisory role
stories.summary: Dodgers executive Bob Wolfe will transition to an advisory role after 14 years as executive vice president and five as chief operating officer.
stories.body:
LOS ANGELES -- Dodgers executive Bob Wolfe is retiring at the end of the year after 14 years as executive vice president.

Wolfe also has served as chief operating officer for the last five years, responsible for the team's day-to-day administrative and operational functions. He's also been the club's liaison to Major League Baseball.

He will transition to an advisory role with the team.

Wolfe's 47-year career includes stints with the NBA's Atlanta Hawks, and MLB's Atlanta Braves and Washington Nationals. He helped with the construction and operation of Turner Field in Atlanta and Nationals Park in Washington.

"Having worked 47 years in team sports, I've been more entertained than anyone deserves," Wolfe said in a statement. "It's been a privilege to ride the coattails of so many on- and off-the-field Hall of Famers, will-be Hall of Famers and should-be Hall of Famers."

stories.headline: AFL 2027 fixture: Five must-watch games in the first month
stories.summary: The 2027 AFL fixture has been released. So, to whet your appetite for the upcoming season, we've picked out the five must-watch games from the opening month.
stories.body:
The 2027 AFL fixture has been released. So, to whet your appetite for the upcoming season, we've picked out the five must-watch games from the opening month of action.

Get the popcorn ready and get set to enjoy these absolute belters in the new year.

5. Port Adelaide vs. Western Bulldogs - Round 4, Adelaide Oval, Sunday, April 8, 7:40pm (AEDT)
Make no mistake, when Zak Butters returns to Adelaide Oval to face his old mob for the first time since departing, it's going to be incredibly spicy.

In a move that shocked absolutely nobody, Butters left Port Adelaide during the 2026 trade period, inking a long-term deal with the Western Bulldogs. It's a brutal blow for the Power, and his ex-teammates will be sure to give him a hard time when they share the field in Round 4. You just know it's going to be on for young and old!

The AFL also made the move to schedule this blockbuster game as the closer to next year's Gather Round. It means far more bodies will be in Adelaide that weekend and a greater number of eyeballs on the clash.

4. Hawthorn vs. Geelong - Round 2, MCG, Monday, March 29, 3:15pm (AEDT)
The traditional Easter Monday clash between the Hawks and Cats is always on our shortlist of early season must-watch games, and next year will be no exception.

Both of these clubs are in the premiership window. Both clubs have added high-profile players this offseason. Both clubs have fanbases that bring an electric energy to Easter Monday at the MCG.

This one is also set to be a fascinating coaching battle between Chris Scott and Sam Mitchell, two of the game's best tacticians, who will go head-to-head just as much as the players on the field.

3. Fremantle vs. Western Bulldogs - Round 1, Optus Stadium, Thursday, March 18, 8:10pm (AEDT)
This Round 1 game in the west is simply oozing with intrigue.

Of course, the question on everyone's mind is how the Dockers back up after having this year's premiership ripped away from them in harrowing circumstances. Does it galvanise the club? Will we see 'Wharfie Time'? Surely not!

For the Bulldogs, they landed the biggest fish of the off-season in superstar midfielder Zak Butters. This will be the first opportunity to watch him play in his new colours, lining up in the middle alongside skipper Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards.

2. Brisbane vs. Collingwood - Round 2, Gabba, Thursday, March 25, 7:50pm (AEDT)
Reigning premier Brisbane will unfurl its latest flag in Round 2 when it hosts Collingwood in its first home game of the season, a clash that has blockbuster written all over it.

The Lions are looking to become just the second team ever to win four consecutive flags (joining, you guessed it, Collingwood from 1927 to 1930) but will be doing it without superstar midfielder Lachie Neale. The two-time Brownlow medallist departed for the Magpies this offseason, making this early season contest between the two clubs extra intriguing.

Plus, any opportunity to watch current Brownlow medallist Nick Daicos play footy is reason in itself to tune in!

1. Hawthorn vs. Brisbane - Round 1, MCG, Friday, March 19, 7:40pm (AEDT)
Thankfully we don't have to wait long for the Hawks and Lions -- quite possibly the competition's two best teams -- to square off in 2027. And if this game delivers even 70% of what these sides dished up in this year's epic preliminary final, then we're in for an absolute treat!

Many have labelled Brisbane's thrilling win over Hawthorn this past September as the greatest game of footy played this century. That in itself should be enough of a reason for their next clash to simply be must-watch.

There will be extra intrigue with both teams given this clash falls in Round 1. For the Lions, they will be looking to navigate life without both superstar midfielder Lachie Neale and master coach Chris Fagan, while the Hawks will be attempting to integrate recruits Zach Merrett and Ben King into their line-up.

stories.headline: Lens fans banned from Liverpool match for throwing flares vs. Brugge
stories.summary: Fans of Ligue 1 club Lens were banned from buying tickets for a Champions League game at Liverpool by a UEFA disciplinary ruling Tuesday.
stories.body:
NYON, Switzerland -- Fans of Ligue 1 club Lens were banned from buying tickets for a Champions League game at Liverpool by a UEFA disciplinary ruling on Tuesday.

Lens fans lit dozens of flares and threw some toward rival supporters and the field, forcing the team's Champions League game at Club Brugge last week to be stopped briefly. Lens lost 3-0.

The club already were on probation by UEFA for fans lighting flares and fireworks at a previous Champions League game at Slavia Prague in September.

UEFA said its appeals judges imposed a ban on Lens selling tickets to fans for two Champions League away games.

The sanction will be served when Lens play at Leipzig on Nov. 24 and at Liverpool at Anfield on Jan. 27. A third game ban is deferred for a two-year probationary period.

UEFA said Lens were fined €80,000 ($89,000) for charges of "lighting and throwing of pyrotechnics as well as for acts of damage."

stories.headline: England's World Cup all but over despite win over PNG
stories.summary: England have beaten Papua New Guinea in a do-or-die encounter but seemingly not by nearly enough to keep their Rugby League World Cup hopes alive.
stories.body:
England's Rugby League World Cup campaign has seemingly ended despite a win - and in a whimper.

Barring a sporting miracle, England can start packing for home despite posting a 34-12 victory over Papua New Guinea in Wollongong on Friday night.

Under the complex tournament format, Brian McDermott's team needed at least a 69-point win to be sure of scraping into the semi-finals.

Now England need Tonga to thrash Samoa by 47 points or more in the fierce Pasifika derby at the same venue on Sunday night.

Given Samoa pumped Tonga 34-6 in last year's Pacific Championships, such a result seems most improbable.

England have only themselves to blame for landing in such a precarious, seemingly hopeless, position.

After losing 30-12 to Tonga in their tournament opener, then not quite atoning with a 82-0 thrashing of France to keep their semi-finals hopes flickering, England made a promising enough start at WIN Stadium.

Realistically needing to score close to a point a minute to apply the pressure on Samoa and Tonga, England were on track after racing to a 22-0 lead after 20 minutes through tries to Matty Ashton, AJ Brimson, Dom Young and Harry Smith.

But then they imploded, making endless errors in pursuit of more points under pressure.

Instead of going on with the job, after leading 24-0 at the break following a 40th-minute penalty goal to Sydney Roosters star Hugo Savala, England completely unravelled.

PNG tries to Dudley Dotoi and Gairo Voro in the opening 10 minutes of the second half piled the pressure on the English - and they crumbled with error after error.

A desperate try in the penultimate minute to Mikey Lewis was little more than an academic consolation for England.
